'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Delaware|Governor]] | before_election = [[John Carney (Delaware politician)|John Carney]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Matt Meyer]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} The '''2024 Delaware gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[governor of Delaware]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[John Carney (Delaware politician)|John Carney]] was [[Term limit|term-limited]] and could not seek re-election to a third term in office. Primary elections took place on September 10, 2024, in which Democratic [[New Castle County, Delaware|New Castle County]] Executive [[Matt Meyer]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state representative [[Mike Ramone]] won their parties' nominations.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-08-06 |website=www.ncsl.org |archive-date=August 17, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230817074608/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |url-status=live }} Meyer comfortably won the election, albeit by the closest margin since [[2004 Delaware gubernatorial election|2004]]. Meyer's 56% of the vote is the lowest for the Democrats since that election, while Ramone's 44% is the highest since for Republicans. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Indiana|Governor]] | before_election = [[Eric Holcomb]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Mike Braun]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Indiana}} The '''2024 Indiana gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the next [[governor of Indiana]], concurrently with the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2024|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] and the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2024 United States elections#State elections|state]] and local elections. Republican Senator [[Mike Braun]] won his first term in office, defeating Democrat former [[Indiana Superintendent of Public Instruction|state Superintendent of Public Instruction]] [[Jennifer McCormick]]. He succeeded Republican incumbent [[Eric Holcomb]], who was term-limited and could not seek a third consecutive term. Primary elections took place on May 7, 2024, in which Republican [[United States Senate|U.S. Senator]] [[Mike Braun]], [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former [[Indiana Superintendent of Public Instruction|state Superintendent of Public Instruction]] [[Jennifer McCormick]], and [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] software engineer Donald Rainwater won their respective parties' nominations.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-05-13 |website=www.ncsl.org |archive-date=December 24, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251224083150/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |url-status=live }} Braun defeated McCormick with 54.4 percent of the vote in the general election.{{cite news |title=Indiana Governor Election Results 2024: McCormick vs. Braun |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-indiana-governor.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=The New York Times |date=November 5, 2024 |archive-date=November 6, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241106002514/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-indiana-governor.html |url-status=live }} Despite this, McCormick's performance marked a significant improvement from that of [[Woody Myers]] in the [[2020 Indiana gubernatorial election|2020 election]]. 2024 Missouri gubernatorial election.text:

'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Missouri|Governor]] | before_election = [[Mike Parson]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Mike Kehoe]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Missouri}} The '''2024 Missouri gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[governor of Missouri]], concurrently with the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2024|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2024 United States elections#State elections|state]] and local elections. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Mike Parson]] was term-limited and could not seek re-election to a second full term in office due to having served more than two years of predecessor [[Eric Greitens]]'s unexpired term following his resignation in June 2018. The Republican nominee, incumbent lieutenant governor [[Mike Kehoe]], defeated the Democratic nominee, minority Leader of the [[Missouri House of Representatives]] [[Crystal Quade]], to succeed Parson. Primary elections took place on August 6, 2024.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-08-06 |website=www.ncsl.org}} [[Mike Kehoe]], the incumbent [[Lieutenant Governor of Missouri|lieutenant governor]], won the Republican nomination, while [[Crystal Quade]], the Minority Leader of the [[Missouri House of Representatives]], won the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nomination.{{Cite news |date=2024-08-06 |title=Missouri Governor Primary Election Results |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/08/06/us/elections/results-missouri-governor-primary.html |access-date=2024-10-27 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Kehoe defeated Quade in the general election with 59.1 percent of the vote.{{cite news |title=Missouri Governor Election Results 2024: Quade vs. Kehoe |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-missouri-governor.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=The New York Times |date=November 5, 2024}} A former [[Missouri bellwether|bellwether state]], Missouri has politically trended rightward in recent years and is today a Republican stronghold at both the federal and state levels. The last Democrat to hold the office of governor in Missouri was [[Jay Nixon]], who comfortably won re-election in [[2012 Missouri gubernatorial election|2012]]. In [[2020 Missouri gubernatorial election|2020]], Parson won by 16.41%, the first time a Republican gubernatorial candidate won by a double-digit margin since [[John Ashcroft]]'s landslide re-election in [[1988 Missouri gubernatorial election|1988]].{{doubtful|date=June 2025}} Major news organizations predicted that the state would elect another Republican governor in 2024.{{Cite web |title=270toWin - 2024 Presidential Election Interactive Map |url=https://www.270towin.com/ |access-date=2024-03-25 |website=270toWin.com}} Kehoe's 20.4 point margin of victory is the largest for a Republican in an open-seat Missouri gubernatorial election since [[Reconstruction era|Reconstruction]]. {{toclimit|3}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Mike Kehoe]], {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Montana|Governor]] | before_election = [[Greg Gianforte]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Greg Gianforte]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 76.57%{{decrease}}4.76{{cite web |url=https://electionresults.mt.gov/VoterTurnoutDetails.aspx|title=Montana Voter Turnout|newspaper=Montana Secretary of State - Christi Jacobsen|date=19 December 2024 |access-date=2025-07-23}} }} {{Elections in Montana}} The '''2024 Montana gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[governor of Montana|governor]] of the U.S. state of [[Montana]], concurrently with the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[2024 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], elections to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2024 United States elections#State elections|state]] and local elections. Primary elections took place on June 4, 2024.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-08-06 |publisher=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}} Incumbent [[Montana Republican Party|Republican]] Governor [[Greg Gianforte]] won election to a second term, defeating [[Montana Democratic Party|Democratic]] nominee Ryan Busse. Gianforte won by a 20% margin, which was larger than his 13% margin in [[2020 Montana gubernatorial election|2020]].{{Cite web |date=2024-06-05 |title=Busse and Gianforte win their respective primary races |url=https://www.krtv.com/news/montana-politics/busse-and-gianforte-win-their-respective-primary-races |access-date=2024-10-27 |website=KRTV NEWS Great Falls |language=en}} Though Montana has backed Republicans in every presidential election since [[1996 United States presidential election in Montana|1996]], the sparsely populated [[Mountain state]] maintained a Democratic tendency at the state and U.S. Senate levels well through the 2010s. This was the first gubernatorial election since [[1996 Montana gubernatorial election|1996]] that a Republican was re-elected governor of Montana. This was also the largest margin of victory in a gubernatorial election since [[Brian Schweitzer]]'s 33-point re-election victory in [[2008 Montana gubernatorial election|2008]], and the largest for a Republican since [[Mark Racicot]]'s aforementioned 58-point landslide re-election in [[1996 Montana gubernatorial election|1996]]. {{toclimit|4}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Greg Gianforte]], incumbent governor (2021–present){{cite news |work=[[KFYR-TV]] |access-date=January 17, 2024 |url=https://www.kfyrtv.com/2024/01/17/governor-greg-gianforte-seek-reelection/ |date=January 17, 2024 |author=Anthony, Michael |title=Governor Greg Gianforte to seek reelection}} **Running mate: [[Kristen Juras]], incumbent lieutenant governor (2021–present) ==== Eliminated in primary ==== *[[Tanner Smith (politician)|Tanner Smith]], [[Montana House of Representatives|state representative]] (2023–present){{cite web |last1=Larson |first1=Seaborn |title=Freshman GOP Rep. announces run for governor |url=https://helenair.com/news/state-regional/government-politics/tanner-smith-candidate-for-montana-governor/article_cb34eb00-0a0b-11ee-afe3-b7a14a35295c.html |website=[[Independent Record]] |date=13 June 2023}} **Running mate: Randy Pinocci, member of the [[Montana Public Service Commission]] (2019–present){{Cite web |author1=Kimbel-Sannit, Arren |author2=Sakariassen, Alex |author3=Eggert, Amanda |date=2024-04-15 |title=Who's running for office in Montana's 2024 election |url=http://montanafreepress.org/2024/04/15/whos-running-state-federal-office-montana-2024-election/ |access-date=2024-05-02 |website=[[Montana Free Press]] |language=en-US}} === Endorsements === {{Endorsements box|title=Greg Gianforte|list=;Organizations *[[National Rifle Association Political Victory Fund]]{{Cite web |last=NRA-PVF |title=NRA-PVF {{!}} Grades {{!}} Montana |url=https://www.nrapvf.org/grades/montana |access-date=2024-05-13 |website=NRA-PVF |language=en}} *[[Susan B. '''Robinson:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}}
{{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of North Carolina|Governor]] | before_election = [[Roy Cooper]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Josh Stein]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }}{{Elections in North Carolina sidebar}} The '''2024 North Carolina gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[governor of North Carolina]]. It was held concurrently with the [[2024 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2024 presidential election]] and [[2024 North Carolina elections|other elections]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state attorney general [[Josh Stein]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] lieutenant governor [[Mark Robinson (American politician)|Mark Robinson]]. He succeeded Democratic incumbent [[Roy Cooper]], who was term-limited. Primary elections took place on March 5, 2024.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=August 6, 2023 |website=ncsl.org}} Stein won the Democratic nomination with 70% of the vote over former state Supreme Court Justice [[Michael R. Morgan]] and Robinson won the Republican nomination with 65% of the vote over state treasurer [[Dale Folwell]]. Initially a tight race, Robinson's history of controversial statements and revelations of comments he made on a pornographic website led to Stein gaining a significant polling advantage. Stein went on to win the election by 14.8 percentage points, the largest margin for a gubernatorial candidate in North Carolina since [[Jim Hunt]] in [[1980 North Carolina gubernatorial election|1980]], as well as winning counties that had not voted Democratic since [[2008 North Carolina gubernatorial election|2008]] ([[Franklin County, North Carolina|Franklin]] and [[Jackson County, North Carolina|Jackson]]), [[2004 North Carolina gubernatorial election|2004]] ([[Alamance County, North Carolina|Alamance]], [[Brunswick County, North Carolina|Brunswick]], and [[Transylvania County, North Carolina|Transylvania]]), and [[1980 North Carolina gubernatorial election|1980]] ([[Cabarrus County, North Carolina|Cabarrus]] and [[Henderson County, North Carolina|Henderson]]). Stein was also the only Democrat in 2024 to win a gubernatorial race in a state [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|concurrent presidential race]]. Robinson became the first Republican gubernatorial candidate since [[1976 North Carolina gubernatorial election|1976]] to not flip a county in the state. Stein received more than three million votes, the most of any candidate in the history of statewide elections in North Carolina. He is the first Jewish governor of the state.{{cite news|url=https://www.jpost.com/us-elections/article-827760|title=Josh Stein defeats Mark Robinson to become North Carolina's first Jewish governor|publisher=The Jerusalem Post|accessdate=November 5, 2024}} Analysts have credited Stein's large margin of victory with [[Coattail effect|helping]] down-ballot Democrats in [[2024 North Carolina elections|concurrent elections]]. Stein received 354,121 more votes than Harris, while Robinson received 657,114 votes less than Trump.{{cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2024/11/north-carolina-election-democrats-governor-legislature/680570/|title=Democrats Actually Had Quite a Good Night in North Carolina|publisher=The Atlantic|accessdate=November 17, 2024}}{{cite news|url=https://apnews.com/article/north-carolina-election-democrats-governor-stein-1548a39fc2207f187785d3a65b217b89|title=North Carolina Democrats find electoral success further down the ballot and hope to build on it|publisher=Associated Press|accessdate=November 17, 2024}} According to exit polls, Stein won independent voters by 23 percentage points, which contributed to Robinson's defeat. Following his loss, Robinson retired from politics. == Background == A typical [[swing state]], North Carolina is considered to be a [[Red states and blue states|purple to slightly red]] southern state at the federal level. Both [[United States Senate|U.S. senators]] from the state are members of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]]. Democrats and Republicans both hold multiple statewide offices in North Carolina. In the [[2020 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2020 presidential election]], [[Donald Trump]] carried North Carolina by 1.34 percentage points, the smallest margin among the states he won.{{Cite web |date=November 8, 2022 |title=Republican Ted Budd wins North Carolina's U.S. Senate race |url=https://apnews.com/article/north-carolina-senate-race-2022-midterm-elections-73fbfc2a6b07c87097b730bd44d42db9 |access-date=March 19, 2023 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}} Incumbent [[Roy Cooper]] was first elected in [[2016 North Carolina gubernatorial election|2016]], defeating then-incumbent governor [[Pat McCrory]] by about 0.2 points. Cooper was re-elected in [[2020 North Carolina gubernatorial election|2020]] by 4.5 percentage points.{{cite web |title=State Composite Abstract Report - Contest.pdf |url=https://s3.amazonaws.com/dl.ncsbe.gov/State_Board_Meeting_Docs/2020-11-24/Canvass/State%20Composite%20Abstract%20Report%20-%20Contest.pdf |website=North Carolina State Board of Elections |access-date=November 24, 2020}}{{cite web |date=November 8, 2016 |title=North Carolina Official General Election Results |url=http://er.ncsbe.gov/?election_dt=11/08/2016&county_id=0&office=COS&contest=0 |access-date=January 5, 2017 |publisher=North Carolina State Board of Elections}} The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee was [[Josh Stein]], the incumbent state attorney general. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee was [[Mark Robinson (American politician)|Mark Robinson]], the incumbent lieutenant governor.{{Cite web |last=Schneider |first=Elena |title=North Carolina AG Josh Stein launches bid for governor |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/01/18/north-carolina-ag-josh-stein-launches-bid-for-governor-00078281 |access-date=March 19, 2023 |website=Politico |date=January 18, 2023 |language=en}} The 2024 election was initially expected to be competitive due to the state's nearly even to slightly right-leaning partisan lean, the concurrent presidential election, and the seat being open due to term limits. However, Robinson later became embroiled in numerous controversies after becoming the nominee, allowing Stein to open up a large and consistent lead in polls. Stein won 37 counties and Robinson won 63. Of the three gubernatorial races that went blue in 2024, North Carolina went bluest in its overall margin, even though the other two were significantly more Democratic states.{{cite news |last1=Cunningham |first1=Eric |title=Ratings Update: Mark Robinson Scandals Shift North Carolina Gubernatorial Race Shifts to Safe Democratic |url=https://elections-daily.com/2024/09/19/ratings-update-robinson-allegations-shift-north-carolina-gubernatorial-race-shifts-to-safe-democratic/ |access-date=September 19, 2024 |work=Elections Daily |date=September 19, 2024}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Josh Stein]], [[North Carolina Attorney General]] (2017–2025) ==== Eliminated in primary ==== * Chrelle Booker, [[Tryon, North Carolina|Tryon]] city councilor (2019–present) and candidate for U.S. Senate in [[2022 United States Senate election in North Carolina|2022]]{{cite news |work=[[Tryon Daily Bulletin]] |access-date=December 9, 2023 |url=https://www.tryondailybulletin.com/2023/12/07/tryon-councilwoman-eyes-north-carolina-governor-seat/ |date=December 7, 2023 |author=Langston, Grant |title=Tryon councilwoman eyes North Carolina governor seat}} * Gary Foxx, former [[Princeville, North Carolina|Princeville]] police chief{{cite web |last1=Mikkelsen |first1=Emily |last2=Melrose |first2=Justyn |title=Election 2024 North Carolina: These are the candidates who filed for races impacting the Piedmont Triad |url=https://myfox8.com/news/politics/your-local-election-hq/election-2024-north-carolina-these-are-the-candidates-who-filed-for-races-impacting-the-piedmont-triad/ |publisher=[[WGHP]] |access-date=December 18, 2023 |date=December 15, 2023}} * [[Michael R. With the backing of former President [[Donald Trump]], Robinson received heavy criticism from Democrats over statements on abortion rights, LGBTQ rights, and education. Robinson had also made a series of controversial statements before and after taking public office, including engaging in [[Holocaust denial]].{{Cite web |title= Republican Mark Robinson and Democrat Josh Stein will face off in North Carolina's governor race| website=[[NBC News]] | date=March 6, 2024 | url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/north-carolina-primary-governor-win-election-rcna141270 |access-date = April 21, 2024}} Robinson also received criticism from some Republicans considered to be moderate, including Senator [[Thom Tillis]] and primary opponent [[Dale Folwell]], both of whom declined to endorse Robinson.{{Cite web |title= State treasurer declines to endorse fellow Republican for governor| date=April 2, 2024 | url=https://ncnewsline.com/2024/04/02/state-treasurer-declines-to-endorse-fellow-republican-for-governor/ |access-date = April 21, 2024}} On September 17, Stein refused any potential debates with Robinson following a challenge from him.{{Cite web |title=Josh Stein won't debate Mark Robinson after lieutenant governor posts X video calling for one |date=September 17, 2024 |url=https://myfox8.com/news/politics/nc-gov-race/lieutenant-governor-mark-robinson-calls-for-debate-with-attorney-general-josh-stein-in-x-video/ |access-date=September 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240917203549/https://myfox8.com/news/politics/nc-gov-race/lieutenant-governor-mark-robinson-calls-for-debate-with-attorney-general-josh-stein-in-x-video/ |archive-date=September 17, 2024 |url-status=dead}} ====Calls for Robinson to drop out==== On September 19, [[CNN]] released a story detailing [[Racism|racist]], [[antisemitism|antisemitic]], [[Misogyny|misogynistic]], and other "disturbing comments" made by an account suspected to be Robinson on a [[pornography]] website between 2008 and 2012.{{cite web |last1=Kaczynski |first1=Andrew |last2=Steck |first2=Em |title=Mark Robinson, NC GOP nominee for governor, called himself a 'black NAZI!,' supported slavery in past comments made on porn forum |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/09/19/politics/kfile-mark-robinson-black-nazi-pro-slavery-porn-forum/index.html |website=[[CNN]] |access-date=September 19, 2024 |language=en |date=September 19, 2024}} Hours later, CNN specified multiple comments made on pornography website message boards, including Robinson calling himself a "[[Morenazi|black NAZI]]" and expressing support for reinstating [[Slavery in the United States|slavery]].{{cite web |title='I'm a black NAZI!': NC GOP nominee for governor made dozens of disturbing comments on porn forum |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/09/19/politics/kfile-mark-robinson-black-nazi-pro-slavery-porn-forum/index.html |website=CNN |access-date=September 19, 2024 |date=September 19, 2024}} The ''[[Carolina Journal]]'' had reported that earlier in the week the [[Donald Trump 2024 presidential campaign|Trump–Vance campaign]] privately told Robinson that he was not welcome at rallies for [[Donald Trump]] or [[JD Vance]].{{cite web |last1=Staff |first1=CJ |title=Robinson under pressure to withdraw from gubernatorial race |url=https://www.carolinajournal.com/robinson-under-pressure-to-withdraw-from-gubernatorial-race/?utm_source=Twitter&utm_medium=BreakingNewsAlert |website=Carolina Journal |access-date=September 19, 2024 |date=September 19, 2024}} This occurred on the same day as the filing deadline for North Carolina's [[2024 United States elections|2024 election]] ballots. Before the story was released, Robinson released a video dismissing the report as "tabloid lies" and saying that he would not drop out of the race.{{cite web |author=WRAL Staff |title=Republican Mark Robinson facing pressure to suspend gubernatorial campaign |url=https://www.wcnc.com/article/news/politics/north-carolina-politics/mark-robinson-under-pressure-drop-out-north-carolina-gubernatorial-race/275-00f8e373-d847-4a92-9b45-81ff2f788bd3 |website=WRAL |access-date=September 19, 2024 |date=September 19, 2024}} His campaign canceled events in [[Henderson, North Carolina|Henderson]] and [[Norlina, North Carolina|Norlina]] planned for the same day. Republican [[North Carolina Senate|state senate]] nominee Scott Lassiter was the first on the ballot with Robinson to call for him to "step aside".{{cite web |title=NC Lt. Gov. Mark Robinson says 'tabloid lies' won't force him out of governor's race |url=https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article292712424.html |website=The News & Observer |access-date=September 19, 2024 |date=September 19, 2024}} Republican North Carolina senator [[Ted Budd]] said, "the allegations are concerning but we don't have any facts".{{cite web |title=Lt. Gov. Mark Robinson under pressure to drop out of NC gubernatorial race |url=https://www.cbs17.com/news/north-carolina-news/lt-gov-mark-robinson-under-pressure-to-drop-out-of-nc-gubernatorial-race/amp/ |website=CBS 17 |access-date=September 19, 2024 |date=September 19, 2024}} That afternoon, ''[[Politico]]'' reported that an email address belonging to Robinson was registered on [[Ashley Madison]], a website designed for people seeking affairs while married.{{cite web |last1=Allison |first1=Natalie |title=Email address belonging to Mark Robinson found on Ashley Madison |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/09/19/north-carolina-lt-governor-mark-robinson-ashley-madison-00180107 |website=Politico |access-date=September 19, 2024 |date=September 19, 2024}} The deadline for Robinson to withdraw from the race or be removed from the ballot passed on the morning of September 20.{{cite news |title=Mark Robinson to stay in North Carolina race despite revelation of offensive comments |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2024/sep/20/north-carolina-mark-robinson |website=[[The Guardian]] |date=September 20, 2024 |access-date=September 20, 2024 |last1=Oladipo '''Piepkorn:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}}
{{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of North Dakota|Governor]] | before_election = [[Doug Burgum]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Kelly Armstrong]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in North Dakota}} The '''2024 North Dakota gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[governor of North Dakota]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Doug Burgum]] decided to not seek a third term and [[Doug Burgum 2024 presidential campaign|ran for president]]. North Dakota is a Republican stronghold, and the [[North Dakota Democratic–Nonpartisan League Party|Democratic–Nonpartisan League (NPL) Party]] has not won a gubernatorial race in the state since [[1988 North Dakota gubernatorial election|1988]]. The Republican nominee, U.S. representative [[Kelly Armstrong]], was elected to his first term, defeating the Democratic–NPL nominee, state senator [[Merrill Piepkorn]] in a landslide. Armstrong was sworn in to office in December 2024, succeeding Burgum, who was subsequently appointed [[United States Secretary of the Interior|Secretary of the Interior]] by [[Donald Trump]] following Trump's victory in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. {{toclimit|3}} ==Background== In November 2022, voters in the state approved a constitutional amendment limiting governors to two four-year terms, but it only applies to individuals elected after January 1, 2023, so incumbent governor [[Doug Burgum]] was still eligible to run for re-election under a [[grandfather clause]].{{Cite web |last=MacPherson|first=James |date=November 8, 2022 |title=North Dakota voters OK term limits for governor, legislators |url=https://apnews.com/article/bismarck-north-dakota-term-limits-government-and-politics-ebba348663d0a8e715f9b90714602354 |access-date=November 20, 2022 |work=Associated Press News}} On June 7, 2023, Burgum announced that he would instead [[2024 Republican Party presidential primaries|run for the Republican nomination]] for [[president of the United States]] in [[2024 United States presidential election|2024]], a race he dropped out of on December 4, 2023. Despite considering running for a third term after the end of his presidential campaign, Burgum announced he would not run for a third term on January 22, 2024. Before Burgum's announcement, former state Senator and former [[2018 United States House of Representatives election in North Dakota|congressional candidate]] [[Tom Campbell (North Dakota politician)|Tom Campbell]] suggested at and considered a gubernatorial run, despite whatever choice Burgum made.{{cite web |last1=Thaden |first1=Geoff |title=Tom Campbell Poised to Enter Governor's Race Regardless of Doug Burgum's Decision on Reelection |url=https://www.wdayradionow.com/news/regional-news/71640-tom-campbell-poised-to-enter-governors-race-regardless-of-doug-burgums |publisher=[[WDAY (AM)]] |access-date=26 January 2024 |date=4 January 2024}}{{cite web |last1=Port |first1=Rob |title=Port: Former state Sen. Tom Campbell sounds like he's ready to be governor |url=https://www.inforum.com/opinion/columns/port-former-state-sen-tom-campbell-sounds-like-hes-ready-to-be-governor |work=[[The Forum of Fargo-Moorhead]] |access-date=26 January 2024 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231215005734/https://www.inforum.com/opinion/columns/port-former-state-sen-tom-campbell-sounds-like-hes-ready-to-be-governor |archive-date=15 December 2023 |date=15 December 2023 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription}} After the decision from Burgum to not seek re-election, Campbell entered the race. On January 23, the day after Burgum's announcement, [[List of United States representatives from North Dakota|U.S. Representative]] [[Kelly Armstrong]] announced he would also seek the governorship, receiving far more reporting than Campbell and an endorsement from Secretary of State [[Michael Howe (politician)|Michael Howe]].{{cite web | Incumbent Republican Gov. [[Chris Sununu]] did not seek election to a fifth term.{{Cite web |date=July 19, 2023 |title=Chris Sununu will not run for re-election for fifth term as New Hampshire governor |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/chris-sununu-new-hampshire-governor-not-running-for-election-2024/ |access-date=July 19, 2023 |website=CBS News |language=en-US}} Primary elections took place on September 10, 2024.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-08-06 |website=NCSL}} [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former U.S. Senator [[Kelly Ayotte]] won the Republican nomination with 63% of the vote over former state senate princess [[Chuck Morse]], and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former Manchester mayor [[Joyce Craig]] won the Democratic nomination with 48% of the vote over state executive councilor [[Cinde Warmington]]. Ayotte won the general election, defeating Craig by a 9.34% margin. The election was the closest gubernatorial race for a U.S. state in the 2024 cycle. Along with neighboring [[2024 Vermont gubernatorial election|Vermont]], this race was one of two Republican-held governorships up for election in 2024 in a state [[Joe Biden]] won in the [[2020 United States presidential election in New Hampshire|2020 presidential election]]. {{toclimit|3}} ==Background== New Hampshire is a Democratic-leaning state in [[New England]] with a pattern of [[split-ticket voting]]. Incumbent Republican governor [[Chris Sununu]] was narrowly elected in [[2016 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|2016]] and won re-election in [[2018 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|2018]], [[2020 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|2020]], and [[2022 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|2022]] despite Republican presidential candidate [[Donald Trump]] losing the state in both [[2016 United States presidential election in New Hampshire|2016]] and [[2020 United States presidential election in New Hampshire|2020]]. Sununu opted not to seek re-election in 2024. This race was widely considered a tossup due to the incumbent retiring, the state's pattern of ticket splitting, and the concurrent [[2024 United States presidential election in New Hampshire|2024 presidential election]].{{Cite web |title=2024 Governor Race ratings |url=https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings/governor-race-ratings |access-date=2023-07-24 |website=The Cook Political Report |language=en}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Kelly Ayotte]], former [[U.S. senator]] (2011–2017){{Cite web |date=2024-09-11 |title=Former Sen. 2024 Utah gubernatorial election.text:

'''King:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of Utah|Governor]] | before_election = [[Spencer Cox]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Spencer Cox]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Utah}} The '''2024 Utah gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[List of governors of Utah|governor of Utah]]. Incumbent Governor [[Spencer Cox]] ran for a second term, winning the Republican primary against state representative [[Phil Lyman]] with 54.4% of the vote; Lyman later mounted a write-in campaign for the general election. Cox won the general election in November, defeating Democratic nominee and state representative [[Brian King (politician)|Brian King]] as well as Lyman.{{cite news |title=Utah Governor Election Results 2024: Cox vs. Smith King |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-utah-governor.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=The New York Times |date=November 5, 2024}} This was the worst performance for a Republican gubernatorial candidate since [[1992 Utah gubernatorial election|1992]], which also saw a major independent candidate. Cox's 24.43% margin of victory was also the smallest since [[2004 Utah gubernatorial election|2004]]. Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Utah since [[1980 Utah gubernatorial election|1980]]. == Background == Utah is considered to be a strongly [[Red states and blue states|red state]] at the federal and state levels: Republicans control all statewide executive offices, the entire congressional delegation, and supermajorities in both state legislative chambers. In the [[2020 United States presidential election in Utah|2020 presidential election]], [[Donald Trump]] carried Utah by 20.5%.{{Cite web |title=Party control of Utah state government |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Utah_state_government |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Utah 2020 presidential election results |url=https://www.cnn.com/election/2020/results/state/utah/president |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=www.cnn.com |language=en}} Cox was first elected in [[2020 Utah gubernatorial election|2020]], defeating Christopher Peterson by 32.65%.{{Cite web |title=Utah 2020 gubernatorial results |url=https://www.cnn.com/election/2020/results/state/utah/governor |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=www.cnn.com |language=en}} ==Republican primary== Incumbent Republican governor [[Spencer Cox (politician)|Spencer Cox]] faced criticism from many conservatives for his moderate political positions, including his veto of HB11,{{cite news |work=[[Politico]] |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/03/22/utah-governor-veto-transgender-sports-ban-00019417 |date=March 22, 2022 |title=Utah governor becomes latest to veto transgender sports ban}} and opposition to former president [[Donald Trump]].{{cite news |access-date=June 24, 2024 |author=Samuel Benson |work=Deseret News |url=https://www.deseret.com/2024/2/15/24074164/utah-gov-cox-republicans-making-a-huge-mistake-if-they-nominate-trump/ |date=February 15, 2024 |title=Utah Gov. Cox: Republicans making 'a huge mistake' if they nominate Trump}} Cox was booed at the Utah Republican state convention in April 2024.{{cite news |access-date=June 24, 2024 |author=Hannah Schoenbaum |work=AP News |url=https://apnews.com/article/utah-republican-governor-debate-cox-lyman-c0844d83cb07d02d8638b4b12dcbec99 |date=June 12, 2024 |title=Utah governor defends record in primary debate after harsh reception at GOP convention}} He faced a primary challenge from state representative [[Phil Lyman]], who won over 67% of the vote at the convention.{{cite news |access-date=June 24, 2024 |author=Brigham Tomco |work=Deseret News |url=https://www.deseret.com/utah/2024/04/27/utah-gop-governor-convention-results/ |date=April 27, 2024 |title=Phil Lyman beats Gov. Spencer Cox at Utah GOP convention. Both advance to primary}} However, Cox collected enough signatures to appear on the primary ballot. Cox consistently led Lyman in polls and won re-nomination, though Lyman refused to concede.{{cite news |author=Bridger Beal-Cvetko |date=June 25, 2024 |title=Spencer Cox cruises to win in GOP primary; Phil Lyman says he won't concede |url=https://www.ksl.com/article/51052654/spencer-cox-cruises-to-win-in-gop-primary-phil-lyman-says-he-wont-concede |work=[[Deseret News]]}}{{cite news |author=Katie McKellar |date=June 25, 2024 |title=AP calls race for Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, but Lyman won't concede |url=https://utahnewsdispatch.com/2024/06/25/race-utah-governor-cox-leads-lyman-republican-primary-election-night-results/ |work=Utah News Dispatch}} ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Spencer Cox (politician)|Spencer Cox]], incumbent governor{{cite news |title=Are Utah Republicans mad at Gov. Incumbent [[Vermont Republican Party|Republican]] governor [[Phil Scott]] won re-election to a fifth term, defeating the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee, [[Vermont Commission on Women]] co-chair [[Esther Charlestin]].{{Cite web |author=Kinzel, Bob |date=2023-10-19 |title=If Gov. Phil Scott runs for reelection, he will remain a Republican |url=https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2023-10-19/if-gov-phil-scott-runs-for-re-election-he-will-remain-a-republican |access-date=2023-11-13 |website=Vermont Public |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Mearhoff |first=Sarah |date=2024-08-13 |title=Esther Charlestin wins Democratic gubernatorial nod while statewide incumbents cruise to primary victories |url=https://vtdigger.org/2024/08/13/most-of-vermonts-statewide-incumbents-cruise-to-easy-primary-victories-tuesday/ |access-date=2024-11-03 |website=VTDigger |language=en-US}}{{cite news|last=Thomas|first=Steff Danielle|date=November 5, 2024|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/4967738-phil-scott-vermont-governor/|title=GOP Gov. Phil Scott wins reelection in blue Vermont|work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|access-date=November 17, 2024}} Primary elections took place on August 13, 2024.{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-08-06 |website=www.ncsl.org}} Being frequently ranked as the nation's most popular governor,{{Cite web |date=2023-07-24 |title=Poll finds Scott retains highest approval rating among governors in US |url=https://www.wcax.com/2023/07/24/poll-finds-scott-retains-highest-approval-rating-among-governors-us/ |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=WCAX News |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Mueller |first=Julia |date=2023-01-12 |title=Here are America’s most popular and least popular governors |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/3811233-here-are-americas-most-popular-and-least-popular-governors/ |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=MultiState |title=Decoding 2023 Gubernatorial Approval Ratings |url=https://www.multistate.us/insider/2023/8/4/decoding-2023-gubernatorial-approval-ratings |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=MultiState |language=en-US}} Scott had won re-election by continually increasing margins since his first election in 2016. Despite Vermont's strong Democratic lean at the presidential level, Scott was expected to easily win again in 2024. Along with [[2024 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|New Hampshire]], this race was one of two Republican-held governorships up for election in 2024 in a state carried by [[Joe Biden]] in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Vermont|2020 presidential election]]. This was the best Republican performance in a Vermont gubernatorial election since [[1946 Vermont gubernatorial election|1946]], with Scott winning every municipality in which votes were cast (as he did in [[2022 Vermont gubernatorial election|2022]]){{cite web |last1=McDonald |first1=Zoe |title=Vermont election updates: Scott, Rodgers and legislative candidates give strong showing |url=https://www.vermontpublic.org/live-updates/vermont-election-results-november-2024 |website=Vermont Public |access-date=17 November 2024}} and Scott's coattails allowed Republicans to break Democratic supermajorities in the state legislature. The [[Nonpartisan blanket primary|top-two primary]] was held on August 6. Incumbent [[Washington State Democratic Party|Democratic]] Governor [[Jay Inslee]] was eligible to seek a fourth term but decided that he would not do so.{{Cite web |last=Furtado |first=David |date=May 1, 2023 |title=Governor Inslee announces he will not seek re-election |url=https://keprtv.com/news/local/governor-inslee-announces-he-will-no-seek-re-election |access-date=May 1, 2023 |publisher=KEPR |language=en}} The Democratic candidate, state Attorney General [[Bob Ferguson (politician)|Bob Ferguson]], defeated the [[Washington State Republican Party|Republican]] candidate, former Congressman [[Dave Reichert]], who conceded defeat on November 19. Ferguson defeated Reichert with 55.51% of the vote in the general election. He also became the first Democrat to win [[Clallam County, Washington|Clallam County]] since [[2000 Washington gubernatorial election|2000]]. This election marked the 11th consecutive victory of the Democratic candidate for governor of Washington. Washington has not had a Republican governor since [[John Spellman]] left office in 1985,{{cite web | url=https://captainstack.medium.com/the-candidates-running-to-be-washingtons-next-governor-61869c44f17a | title=The candidates running to be Washington's next governor | date=February 17, 2024 }} the longest streak of Democratic leadership of any state in the country and the third-longest streak of one-party leadership after [[South Dakota]] (which has not had a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor since [[Harvey Wollman]] left office in 1979) and [[Utah]] (which has not had a Democratic governor since [[Scott M. Matheson|Scott Matheson]] left office nine days prior to Spellman in 1985).{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Benjamin |date=July 19, 2019 |title=Zachary Moses, a Democratic candidate for governor, wants to break up Republican control of Utah and build a space port |url=https://www.sltrib.com/news/politics/2019/07/19/zachary-moses-democratic/ |access-date=August 29, 2019 |work=Salt Lake Tribune}}{{cite news |last1=Scott |first1=Dylan |date=November 7, 2018 |title=Kristi Noem elected first woman governor of South Dakota |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2018/11/7/18055928/midterm-election-results-south-dakota-governor-kristi-noem-winner |access-date=August 26, 2019 |work=Vox}}{{cite news |last1=Camden |first1=Jim |date=January 16, 2018 |title=John Spellman, Washington's last Republican governor, dies |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2018/jan/16/former-gov-spellman-dies/ |access-date=August 23, 2019 |newspaper=The Spokesman-Review}} == Primary election == Washington is one of two states that holds a [[top-two primary]], meaning that all candidates are listed on the same ballot regardless of party affiliation, and the top two advance to the general election. The filing deadline was May 10, 2024. On that day, two candidates named Bob Ferguson entered the race at the behest of a conservative activist who sought people with the same surname as [[Washington Attorney General]] [[Bob Ferguson (politician)|Bob Ferguson]], who was considered the Democratic frontrunner.{{cite news |last=Withycombe |first=Claire |date=May 10, 2024 |title=Three Bob Night: Two more Bob Fergusons running for WA governor |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/politics/three-bob-night-two-more-bob-fergusons-running-for-wa-governor/ |work=The Seattle Times |accessdate=May 14, 2024}} The two new candidates—a retired state employee and a [[U.S. Army]] veteran—resigned from the race on May 13, the deadline to withdraw, after questions about the legality of their campaigns arose. Washington's state statutes prohibit a new candidate with the same surname as an already-filed candidate from running with the intent to confuse or mislead voters.{{cite news |last=Withycombe |first=Claire |date=May 13, 2024 |title=Bob's Your Uncle: 2 Bob Fergusons withdraw from WA governor's race The '''2024 West Virginia gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2024, to elect the [[List of governors of West Virginia|governor of West Virginia]], concurrently with the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2024|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] and elections to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2024 United States elections#State elections|state]] and local elections. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state [[List of attorneys general of West Virginia|Attorney General]] [[Patrick Morrisey]] was elected to his first term in office after defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Huntington, West Virginia|Huntington]] mayor [[Stephen T. Williams|Steve Williams]] in the general election.<ref>{{cite news |title=West Virginia Governor Election Results 2024: Williams vs. Morrisey |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-west-virginia-governor.html |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=The New York Times |date=November 5, 2024}}</ref> Incumbent Republican [[Jim Justice]] was term-limited and was unable to seek re-election to a third consecutive term in office; he instead [[2024 United States Senate election in West Virginia|ran for the U.S. Senate]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=WDTV News |date=2023-04-27 |title=Gov. Justice announces run for U.S. Senate |url=https://www.wdtv.com/2023/04/27/gov-justice-announces-run-us-senate/ |access-date=2023-04-27 |website=www.wdtv.com |language=en |archive-date=April 27, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230427213851/https://www.wdtv.com/2023/04/27/gov-justice-announces-run-us-senate/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

First elected in [[2016 West Virginia gubernatorial election|2016]] as a Democrat by 6.8 percentage points, Justice switched parties in August 2017 and won re-election in [[2020 West Virginia gubernatorial election|2020]] as a Republican by 33.3 percentage points. Primary elections took place on May 14, 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2024 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2023-08-06 |website=www.ncsl.org |archive-date=August 17, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230817074608/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates |url-status=live }}</ref> This is the first time since [[1972 West Virginia gubernatorial election|1972]] that Republicans won consecutive gubernatorial elections in the state.  However, Morrisey performed worse than Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, who outperformed Morrisey by 7.98 percentage points. Meanwhile, Williams outperformed Kamala Harris by 3.48 percentage points. All statewide Democratic nominees failed to carry a single county in their respective general election races in [[2024 West Virginia elections|2024]].

== Background ==
A [[Conservatism in the United States|conservative]] rural southeastern state, West Virginia is considered [[Red states and blue states|extremely Republican]] at the federal and state levels; Republicans hold all statewide executive offices and supermajorities in both state legislative houses, and from 2015 until he became an Independent in 2024, Senator Joe Manchin had been the state's only congressional Democrat. In the [[2020 United States presidential election in West Virginia|2020 presidential election]], [[Donald Trump]] carried West Virginia by 38.93 percentage points.

With Jim Justice term-limited and unable to run for a third consecutive term as Governor, the Republican primary was expected to be competitive and crowded. Most analysts considered Republicans to be a heavy favorite, given the state's partisan lean and the margin from the previous election.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-28 |title=West Virginia GOP auditor announces 2024 run for governor |url=https://apnews.com/article/west-virginia-governor-2024-election-mccuskey-cb9b7c25310eb5d0289cd6cb33456737 |access-date=2023-03-02 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}}</ref>
